issues.failure_explanation: Equation (3.3) in Theorem 3.1 states that the probability density function rho of (u, v) on R_+^d x R^d equals the probability density function p of (y, z, v) on R^(3d) at u = (y^2 + z^2)^(1/2). However, transforming Cartesian coordinates (y_i, z_i) to 2D polar coordinates with radial coordinate u_i = (y_i^2 + z_i^2)^(1/2) introduces the Jacobian area element dy_i dz_i = u_i du_i dtheta_i. Integrating out the angular variables over [0, 2pi)^d means rho(t,(u,v)) = (2pi)^d (prod_{i=1}^d u_i) p(t,(y,z,v)). Omitting this Jacobian factor is mathematically false, as the unweighted p does not integrate to 1 with respect to du dv on R_+^d x R^d.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Correct equation (3.3) to \rho(t,(u,v)) = (2\pi)^d \left(\prod_{i=1}^d u_i\right) p(t,(y,z,v)) and clarify in the proof of Theorem 3.4 that the Jacobian factor cancels when taking Radon-Nikodym derivatives with respect to the invariant measures.
issues.overall_effect: Equation (3.3) is false as stated. In Theorem 3.4, the proof invokes p = rho directly, though the ratio rho/pi = p/pi_{3d} remains unchanged because the same Jacobian factor appears in both densities.
issues.title: Missing Jacobian determinant factor equating Cartesian and polar/cylindrical probability densities
issues.why_classification: A routine local correction adding the standard polar Jacobian factor resolves the defect without weakening any theorem or requiring new proof architecture.

issues.failure_explanation: Proposition 3.4 asserts that z_t = (eta_t, x_t) satisfies the Riemannian Langevin equation with metric g = M^{-1} and drift -M grad H + div_g(M). By direct computation from Ito's formula, the true drift of z_t is mu(z) = -M grad H + [3/2, x/(2 eta)]^T. However, evaluating the paper's definition of Riemannian divergence div_g(M) = |g|^{-1/2} sum_j d_j(M_{.j} |g|^{1/2}) with |g|^{1/2} = (det M)^{-1/2} = 1/(2 eta) yields [1/2, 0]^T. The claim in the proof that mu(z) = -M grad H + 1/2 [1, x/eta]^T = -M grad H + div_{M^{-1}}(M) is false in both components: the actual discrepancy is [3/2, x/(2 eta)]^T, which equals the Euclidean divergence sum_j d_j M_{.j}, not the Riemannian divergence with respect to g.

issues.failure_explanation: Theorem 4.8 claims that the invariant distribution pi_{Delta t} of the numerical scheme converges to pi as Delta t -> 0. The proof attempts to show E_{1,T}(Delta t) -> 0 by applying Theorem 4.4 to \tilde{pi}_{Delta t} = pi_{Delta t}(. cap B_R) / pi_{Delta t}(B_R). However, Theorem 4.4 strictly requires Assumption 4.1(ii): the initial distribution rho_0 must satisfy rho_0 << pi with rho_0/pi uniformly bounded. Restricting pi_{Delta t} to a ball B_R does not establish absolute continuity with respect to pi, nor does it bound the density ratio \tilde{pi}_{Delta t}/pi (which can diverge near u_i = 0 where pi vanishes while pi_{Delta t} is supported away from 0). Furthermore, \tilde{pi}_{Delta t} depends on Delta t, so applying Theorem 4.4 requires a uniform-in-Delta t bound on \|\tilde{pi}_{Delta t}/pi\|_\infty, which is completely unproved. Consequently, E_{1,T}(Delta t) -> 0 is unsupported, and the proof of convergence of the invariant measures fails.
